title: Chapter 37 — 'I Need to Think About It'
intro: The vaguest objection on the floor — the sorting question and the structured think.

sections.title: Agree, Then Isolate
sections.content:
When a customer says 'I need to think about it,' what they usually mean is one of three things: they have a concern they have not voiced, they genuinely need spousal input, or they are not convinced the product is right for them.

Your first move: agree with them. 'Absolutely — this is a significant purchase and you should feel confident.' Then gently identify the real concern.

The isolate technique: 'I completely understand. Just so I can help — is it the product itself, or is it more about the timing or the investment?' This separates product objection from price objection from authority objection. Each one has a different response.

sections.title: Address the Real Concern
sections.content:
If it is the product: 'What would you need to see or know to feel confident this is the right one?' Then address it directly with evidence.

If it is the price: transition to the price objection framework. Offer a financing option. Break the price into monthly: 'Over the 10-year life of this dishwasher, the difference between this model and the cheaper one is about $3 a month.'

If it is authority — spouse or partner: 'Would it help if I put together a summary you can share? I can include the specs, the price, and why we landed on this model so your partner has the full picture.'

sections.title: The Quote Hold
sections.content:
Always create the quote before they leave. 'Let me lock this pricing in for you — the promotion expires [date] and I want to make sure you are protected.' This gives you a reason to follow up and creates urgency without pressure.

Never let them walk out without a next step. The close rate on a customer who leaves without a quote and a follow-up appointment drops to under 15 percent.
